title: Parameters for Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric
summary: Explains the parameter and expression system that Fabric Data Factory pipelines use to avoid hard-coded values: how pipeline parameters are declared and referenced, how the @ / @{} expression syntax and string interpolation behave, how a parameter reference resolves to a connection GUID, and the built-in system variables and function families (string, collection, logical, conversion, math, date) available inside expressions.
audience: Data engineers and pipeline developers building reusable, metadata-driven Fabric pipelines instead of one-off, hard-coded ones.
why_it_matters: Parameterization is the mechanical foundation a metadata-driven architecture is built on: without pipeline parameters, dynamic connection references, and system variables to resolve per-run configuration, a single pipeline cannot be driven by an external control table to process many sources.
takeaways: A pipeline parameter is set once per run and stays fixed for the duration of that run, unlike a variable which can change during execution.
The @ / @{} expression syntax, including its escaping rules, is what lets pipeline JSON embed dynamic values inside otherwise static strings.
Connections themselves can be parameterized by substituting a connection's GUID at runtime, which is the mechanism a metadata-driven pipeline uses to point at different sources without redeployment.
A broad library of built-in functions (string, collection, logical, conversion, math, date) is available inside expressions, reducing the need for external transformation logic just to shape a value.
System variables exposed under pipeline() scope give an expression access to run context (run ID, trigger, workspace) without the pipeline author having to pass that context in explicitly.

claims.text: A Fabric Data Factory pipeline parameter is assigned a value when the pipeline run starts and that value remains constant for the rest of the run, distinguishing it from a variable that can be reassigned mid-run.
Expressions in pipeline JSON are marked with a leading @ symbol, and a literal string that itself needs to start with @ must be escaped as @@ so it is not misread as an expression.

Wrapping an expression in @{ } enables string interpolation inside a larger literal string, and the interpolated result is always coerced to a string even if the underlying expression evaluates to a number.
Referencing a pipeline parameter directly with @pipeline().parameters.name (no braces) preserves its native type, such as returning a number as a number rather than a string.
New pipeline parameters are added from the Parameters tab of the pipeline canvas properties pane, where each parameter is given a name, a data type, and a default value.

A connection used inside a pipeline can be parameterized by capturing its GUID connection ID from Manage connections and gateways and substituting that GUID dynamically via a string parameter, letting one pipeline target different connections per run.
Deeply nested activity output can be addressed in an expression using bracket syntax, such as referencing a subfield resolved by another pipeline parameter, rather than only chained dot notation.

Pipeline-scope system variables exposed under pipeline() include the workspace name, pipeline name, run ID, trigger ID, trigger name, and trigger time, giving an expression access to run context without it being passed in as an explicit parameter.

When a pipeline run is invoked by an Execute Pipeline activity from a parent pipeline, the optional system variables TriggeredByPipelineName and TriggeredByPipelineRunId resolve to the parent's name and run ID, and evaluate to null otherwise.
Trigger-related date and time system variables, in both pipeline and trigger scope, are returned as UTC timestamps in ISO 8601 format.

The expression language provides distinct function families for strings, collections (arrays, strings, dictionaries), logical comparisons, type conversion, math, and date/time manipulation, covering common transformation needs directly inside an expression.
